passages: Apple has more than just the iPhone Duo arriving in October, it seems.
The Cupertino-based tech giant has announced another product launch for October 13, playfully captioning it 'Welcome Home.'
Let me know what you’re most excited to see get the ‘Welcome Home’ treatment in the comments.
For the Apple Home — or Apple HomeKit — faithful, this is especially exciting.
The other question surrounds the much-rumored smart display from Apple.
It certainly feels like Apple is hinting at something home-related.

Apple's smart home tech includes, most obviously, the HomePod mini and full-sized HomePod, its smart speakers that play music, ring with alarms, handle calls and FaceTime calls, and bring Siri into the home.
But it also extends to the Apple TV 4K box, a streaming box that brings Apple’s own services and other major streamers to the big screen.
It’s been quite some time since those were all updated or unveiled.

Most recently, a fresh report from Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman teases that Apple might drop some smart home accessories, like a thermostat, smart deadbolt locks, sensors, and cameras, in partnership with LG .
Essentially, LG-made devices purpose-built for Apple Home that will likely fit very well into the existing ecosystem and work with these new devices.
He specializes in covering companies like Apple, Samsung, and Google and going hands-on with mobile devices, smart home gadgets, TVs, and wearables.
In his spare time, you can find Jacob listening to Bruce Springsteen, building a Lego set, or binge-watching the latest from Disney, Marvel, or Star Wars.
Rumors suggest new versions are coming, not redesigns or rethinks, but more power under the hood to let Siri AI work on the devices.
We’ll need to wait and see what Apple unveils to know exactly what it is packing.
The super-cute, robotic smart home display is still likely a good way out.
Though, I can’t be the only one who wants a smart display that resembles the Pixar Lamp, right?
As someone who currently uses HomePod minis, HomePods, and Apple TV 4Ks around my home, this refresh feels long overdue.
These are products that have become pretty integral to how I use Apple at home, but they’ve also felt like they’ve been waiting for their next chapter for a while now.
That’s ultimately what makes this rumored HomePad so interesting to me.
Plenty of smart displays already exist, but Apple has a chance to make one that feels less like another screen in your house and more like a natural extension of the Apple devices you use every day.
Of course, I’m also hoping it sounds good enough to blast some Springsteen on.

Apple has more than just the iPhone Duo arriving in October, it seems. The Cupertino-based tech giant has announced another product launch for October 13, playfully captioning it 'Welcome Home.' For the Apple Home — or Apple HomeKit — faithful, this is especially exciting. The teaser for October 13, 2026, not only has some warmth to it, but it also tees up the long-awaited, much-rumored refresh of its existing Home devices. The video depicts a stitched artwork of the Apple logo in the classic shades, with 'Welcome Home’ inscribed underneath it. It certainly feels like Apple is hinting at something home-related. Apple's smart home tech includes, most obviously, the HomePod mini and full-sized HomePod, its smart speakers that play music, ring with alarms, handle calls and FaceTime calls, and bring Siri into the home. But it also extends to the Apple TV 4K box, a streaming box that brings Apple’s own services and other major streamers to the big screen. It’s been quite some time since those were all updated or unveiled. Rumors suggest new versions are coming, not redesigns or rethinks, but more power under the hood to let Siri AI work on the devices. It wouldn’t just bring them up to the level of competing Amazon Alexa and Google smart speakers, but would make these devices a lot more capable and bring parity to how Siri works on other Apple devices. It’s likely that a new HomePod mini could sport a fresh coat of paint, but the processor change under the hood will be the real power boost. The same goes for a new HomePod or Apple TV 4K. The other question surrounds the much-rumored smart display from Apple. It might be called the ‘HomePad,’ as leaks have suggested — but whatever its name, the teaser video posted by Greg Joswiak (Apple’s SVP of Marketing) suggests it could arrive at the event. ‘Welcome Home’ certainly hints at a new category, and the video’s stitched Apple logo and tagline certainly feels like a pretty deliberate tease for a brand-new device landing. Based on the rumors, the HomePad will likely combine an iPad with a HomePod or HomePod mini, offering a 6-inch display mounted to a base and running a new OS. Siri AI is expected to be the main control method and central to the experience, and it’s likely why it’s only arriving now, since the upgraded assistant launched last month alongside iOS 27. According to rumors, you’ll be able to use the HomePad for smart home control, topical or specific questions with Siri, viewing photos or videos, taking FaceTime calls, and even opening other apps. Like an Echo Show, it’ll apparently tailor the experience for each person, which is essential for a home device. Most recently, a fresh report from Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman teases that Apple might drop some smart home accessories, like a thermostat, smart deadbolt locks, sensors, and cameras, in partnership with LG . Essentially, LG-made devices purpose-built for Apple Home that will likely fit very well into the existing ecosystem and work with these new devices. We’ll need to wait and see what Apple unveils to know exactly what it is packing. The super-cute, robotic smart home display is still likely a good way out. Though, I can’t be the only one who wants a smart display that resembles the Pixar Lamp, right? As someone who currently uses HomePod minis, HomePods, and Apple TV 4Ks around my home, this refresh feels long overdue. These are products that have become pretty integral to how I use Apple at home, but they’ve also felt like they’ve been waiting for their next chapter for a while now. And when it comes to the rumored smart display, I’m particularly bullish on the idea. Apple’s stance on privacy, combined with how tightly its products already work together, could make this a really compelling home device. Even something as simple as displaying photos from Apple Photos is a nice play. I can also see the appeal of having a display that works seamlessly with your iPhone, Apple Watch , and Mac, while knowing who is using it and tailoring the experience accordingly. That’s ultimately what makes this rumored HomePad so interesting to me. Plenty of smart displays already exist, but Apple has a chance to make one that feels less like another screen in your house and more like a natural extension of the Apple devices you use every day. Of course, I’m also hoping it sounds good enough to blast some Springsteen on. The good thing is, we don’t have long to wait, as Apple’s set this event for October 13, 2026. sources.title: What to expect from Apple’s ‘Welcome Home’ event
passages: We are quickly coming up on Apple’s “Welcome Home” launch event, where we expect a host of smart home-related announcements.
“Welcome Home” will officially kick off in New York on October 13th at 9AM ET.
Both are expected to feature Apple’s N1 chip, which includes support for Wi-Fi and Bluetooth 6.0.

The whole thing will reportedly run a new software platform called… homeOS The company may have registered a trademark for the name through a shell company called Home Operations Suite LLC, a move that Apple has pulled before to quietly secure the rights to names.
A proper smart home hub Until now, Apple has primarily relied on the Home app to control all the various bits and bobs that make up your smart home.
But don’t expect Apple to share too much of the spotlight with its partners.

The new device, which could be called HomePad or HomeView or, more simply, Apple Home Hub, will reportedly feature a 6-inch square touchscreen that can either be mounted on a wall or placed on a table or countertop.
Apple will offer the option for secondary identification through an iPhone to keep personal data more secure.
The OS will also include your usual assortment of Apple apps and widgets, including Apple Music, Podcasts, and News, as well as Reminders, Notes, and Siri AI.

extraction.body: We are quickly coming up on Apple’s “Welcome Home” launch event, where we expect a host of smart home-related announcements. We are expecting refreshes to Apple TV and HomePod Mini, as well as a brand new smart home hub. We could also see the debut of a new platform called homeOS, and some partner devices from LG. What we probably won’t be seeing is the long-rumored touchscreen MacBook, which Cupertino whisperer Mark Gurman says will debut later this month. “Welcome Home” will officially kick off in New York on October 13th at 9AM ET. A proper smart home hub Until now, Apple has primarily relied on the Home app to control all the various bits and bobs that make up your smart home. But it’s a market niche that the company has been eager to tackle more fully. The new device, which could be called HomePad or HomeView or, more simply, Apple Home Hub, will reportedly feature a 6-inch square touchscreen that can either be mounted on a wall or placed on a table or countertop. According to Mark Gurman, the countertop model will somewhat resemble the iMac G4, with the screen attached to an arm set into a half sphere. Apple will offer the option for secondary identification through an iPhone to keep personal data more secure. The whole thing will reportedly run a new software platform called… homeOS The company may have registered a trademark for the name through a shell company called Home Operations Suite LLC, a move that Apple has pulled before to quietly secure the rights to names. The platform will supposedly feature a streamlined interface that “looks like a mashup of iOS, tvOS and watchOS,” according to Gurman. The focus, obviously, will be on smart home applications, like controlling thermostats and smart locks, and it will also be capable of making FaceTime calls. The OS will also include your usual assortment of Apple apps and widgets, including Apple Music, Podcasts, and News, as well as Reminders, Notes, and Siri AI. HomePod Mini and Apple TV get a minor refresh Word is that not much is changing with the HomePod Mini or Apple TV. This will be the first update to the HomePod Mini since it was announced on October 13th of 2020 — exactly six years before Apple’s Welcome Home event. While the company isn’t making any dramatic changes for the Mini’s birthday, it will be offering it in new colors, including green and pink. This will be the first hardware refresh for the Apple TV since 2022. Rumors are that it will have an integrated mic so that you won’t need to talk into the remote or a paired HomePod to control the Apple TV with Siri. Both are expected to feature Apple’s N1 chip, which includes support for Wi-Fi and Bluetooth 6.0. But don’t expect Apple to share too much of the spotlight with its partners. We’ve already seen a leak of LG smart home, including deadbolts, thermostats, and more. They’ll also reportedly include an NFC-based “Proximity Control” that pops up a hint in the iPhone’s Dynamic Island when held near the device, as well as a “tap to set up without power” pairing feature. Update October 11th, 2026: Added additional rumors from Mark Gurman’s Power On newsletter.

coreStoryFacts.text: Apple has more than just the iPhone Duo arriving in October, it seems.
The Cupertino-based tech giant has announced another product launch for October 13, playfully captioning it 'Welcome Home.'
Let me know what you’re most excited to see get the ‘Welcome Home’ treatment in the comments.
For the Apple Home — or Apple HomeKit — faithful, this is especially exciting.
The other question surrounds the much-rumored smart display from Apple.
It certainly feels like Apple is hinting at something home-related.

Apple's smart home tech includes, most obviously, the HomePod mini and full-sized HomePod, its smart speakers that play music, ring with alarms, handle calls and FaceTime calls, and bring Siri into the home.
But it also extends to the Apple TV 4K box, a streaming box that brings Apple’s own services and other major streamers to the big screen.
It’s been quite some time since those were all updated or unveiled.

Most recently, a fresh report from Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman teases that Apple might drop some smart home accessories, like a thermostat, smart deadbolt locks, sensors, and cameras, in partnership with LG .
Essentially, LG-made devices purpose-built for Apple Home that will likely fit very well into the existing ecosystem and work with these new devices.
He specializes in covering companies like Apple, Samsung, and Google and going hands-on with mobile devices, smart home gadgets, TVs, and wearables.
In his spare time, you can find Jacob listening to Bruce Springsteen, building a Lego set, or binge-watching the latest from Disney, Marvel, or Star Wars.
Rumors suggest new versions are coming, not redesigns or rethinks, but more power under the hood to let Siri AI work on the devices.
We’ll need to wait and see what Apple unveils to know exactly what it is packing.
The super-cute, robotic smart home display is still likely a good way out.
Though, I can’t be the only one who wants a smart display that resembles the Pixar Lamp, right?
As someone who currently uses HomePod minis, HomePods, and Apple TV 4Ks around my home, this refresh feels long overdue.
These are products that have become pretty integral to how I use Apple at home, but they’ve also felt like they’ve been waiting for their next chapter for a while now.
That’s ultimately what makes this rumored HomePad so interesting to me.
Plenty of smart displays already exist, but Apple has a chance to make one that feels less like another screen in your house and more like a natural extension of the Apple devices you use every day.
Of course, I’m also hoping it sounds good enough to blast some Springsteen on.

Apple’s stance on privacy, combined with how tightly its products already work together, could make this a really compelling home device. Even something as simple as displaying photos from Apple Photos is a nice play. I can also see the appeal of having a display that works seamlessly with your iPhone, Apple Watch , and Mac, while knowing who is using it and tailoring the experience accordingly. That’s ultimately what makes this rumored HomePad so interesting to me. extraction.body: Study finds coding efficiency gains get “absorbed” by human review “bottleneck.” Anyone who has even tangentially associated with computer programming knows that modern AI coding assistants and agents can be incredibly efficient at generating huge amounts of functional code . But coders making use of those tools also know better than to trust the accuracy of that code , meaning substantial effort needs to be spent reviewing any AI-generated output. A recent study of actual coding practices across hundreds of firms finds that human code review forms a significant “bottleneck” for the overall efficiency of AI coding tools, resulting in “little evidence that firms increase software output or reduce employment” by using them. Any efficiency increased during the actual coding phase, the study authors find, is “absorbed by downstream constraints in the production process”; as “the code review process significantly increases in length, pull requests are more likely to require revisions, and reviewers leave more comments.” To come to these conclusions, Harvard University researchers Fiona Chen and James Stratton made use of aggregated analytics data from Jellyfish , which measures the granular output of engineering teams. That data encompasses 300 million individual “work events” (e.g., commits and pull requests) and issue management software data across more than 700,000 employees at over 700 relevant software development firms from 2021 through March of 2026. To assess the impact of AI tools on these firms, the researchers used a mix of directly measured AI usage and analyses of GitHub activity to determine when each company started introducing either AI coding assistants (which can help auto-complete code primarily authored by humans) and/or AI coding agents (which primarily write and submit code autonomously based on prompts) into their workflows. The researchers then perform some complicated math to determine a “difference of differences” regression on key variables both before and after the introduction of these tools at different points in time across different organizations. In terms of raw code being produced, the results are clear and stark. The introduction of AI coding agents at a firm leads to a 30 percent increase in total lines of code generated, a 20 percent rise in the number of total commits, and a 23 percent increase in pull requests on average, the researchers write. But all that extra code doesn’t translate directly into improved software output on the firm level. On the contrary, the resolution rate for Issues and Epics (i.e. wholesale software features) tracked by tools like Jira did not change in a statistically significant way after AI tools were introduced (the researchers also found no “compositional shift” in the size or complexity of those Jira-tracked issues across the AI introduction). The reason for that discrepancy can be found directly in the code review process, which takes markedly longer on average after the introduction of AI coding agents. Overall, the average “review process” time between a pull request getting submitted and it being merged into the codebase balloons 49 percent on average after AI agents are introduced. That effect can be seen in more granular data, too, with “the share of pull requests with changes requested nearly doubl[ing], and the number of comments per pull request increas[ing] by 35%” following the AI agent shift, the researchers write. In response to this change, the researchers found a 14 percent increase in the share of workers performing code reviews after AI agents’ introduction. They also write that they “cannot attribute significant employment changes to AI” after looking at total active workers across Jellyfish and cross-referencing with LinkedIn data at those firms. While AI could also theoretically help with this review process, the researchers found that, so far, that impact has been marginal. Although 80 percent of measured firms used some form of AI code review by March 2026, AI agents were only responsible for 23.3 percent of all review comments and 10.8 percent of all pull requests, suggesting humans were still responsible for the vast majority of this work. AI agents are still a relatively new part of the coding world, of course, and there have been significant updates and upgrades to their output even since this study’s March 2026 data cutoff. And while 95 percent of firms in the study have implemented AI coding agents by this point, many are doubtlessly still going through a learning process regarding when and how to best deploy them. These kinds of “coding time versus review time” trade-offs could improve as software engineering teams gain more experience with the pros and cons of siccing an AI agent on particular coding problems. For now, though, letting AI write your code looks like a double-edged sword, with increases in coding speed counteracted by similar increases in human code review time and effort. It’s the kind of result that makes us wonder if the considerable time and expense to get AI coding agents working is really worth it for most companies. sources.title: AI Coding Agents Write 30% More Code – and Resolve Zero Additional Issues, Harvard Study Finds - Forkast News
passages: The first large-scale empirical study of AI coding agents at enterprise scale finds that agents boost code volume by 30%, but the gains don't translate to software output.
The bottleneck is code review: review times increase 49%, revision requests nearly double, and AI review tools haven't replaced human oversight.
Researchers Fiona Chen and James Stratton analyzed data from the Jellyfish engineering analytics platform, covering 718 firms and over 725,000 workers between 2021 and 2026.

The findings are stark: while AI agents like Claude Code, Cursor, and Devin have increased code production by 30%-adding nearly 1,500 lines per worker-month-there has been no statistically significant increase in resolved Jira issues or completed epics.
When developers use AI to generate code faster, they are essentially pushing more work into the review queue.
As one senior engineer noted in the study, “We were able to write code faster in some instances, but there is only one bottleneck at a time.
The pattern is clear: firms are rushing to adopt AI agents-with adoption rates climbing from near zero in late 2024 to over 95% by early 2026-without adjusting their internal workflows.
The study found that 14% more workers are now being pulled into the code review process, placing a heavy burden on senior engineers who must vet the influx of AI-generated updates.

extraction.body: Tomorrow, First. News and intelligence for the agentic economy The first large-scale empirical study of AI coding agents at enterprise scale finds that agents boost code volume by 30%, but the gains don't translate to software output. The bottleneck is code review: review times increase 49%, revision requests nearly double, and AI review tools haven't replaced human oversight. Enterprise technology leaders are currently caught in a measurement trap. When evaluating the impact of AI coding agents, the industry has largely focused on the volume of code produced. It is an easy metric to track, but it is increasingly clear that it is the wrong one. By prioritizing output speed, firms are ignoring the reality of how software actually moves from an idea to a finished product. A new Harvard working paper , Artificial Intelligence in the Firm: Bottlenecks in Software Production , provides the first large-scale empirical evidence that this focus on volume is masking a significant operational hurdle. Researchers Fiona Chen and James Stratton analyzed data from the Jellyfish engineering analytics platform, covering 718 firms and over 725,000 workers between 2021 and 2026. The findings are stark: while AI agents like Claude Code, Cursor, and Devin have increased code production by 30%-adding nearly 1,500 lines per worker-month-there has been no statistically significant increase in resolved Jira issues or completed epics. The data reveals a disconnect between activity and outcome. sources.title: AI coding tools help write more lines of code, but not ship more software: study - IT Brew
passages: After examining the data and AI usage telemetry of over 100,000 GitHub developers, researchers from MIT and UPenn’s Wharton School have determined that AI coding tools might help developers produce more lines of code, but that’s not leading to more finished software shipped.

Manav Khurana, GitLab’s chief product and marketing officer, added it’s important for organizations using AI coding tools to invest in agentic infrastructure to support other steps of the software development life cycle: “If they don’t have the right agentic infrastructure to make sure that code created can become shipped software with the right level of automation, they also risk that the new code creates reliability problems, or security problems, or cost overruns, because speed sometimes also brings with it chaos.”
IT Brew caught up with Greg Jennings, VP of engineering and AI at AI-native development company Anaconda, to understand what human bottlenecks stem from leveraging AI tools.
Brianna Monsanto is a reporter for IT Brew who covers news about cybersecurity, cloud computing, and strategic IT decisions made at different companies.
Similar disparities were observed when examining developers who relied on autocomplete tools, which suggest code as the developer types.

extraction.body: Do AI coding tools actually make developers more productive? It depends on how you define productivity. After examining the data and AI usage telemetry of over 100,000 GitHub developers, researchers from MIT and UPenn’s Wharton School have determined that AI coding tools might help developers produce more lines of code, but that’s not leading to more finished software shipped. The researchers found that synchronous agents (agents that write and edit code with the developer in real time) produced a 741% increase in lines of code and led to a 65% increase in pull requests. However, software releases only rose 20%. Similar disparities were observed when examining developers who relied on autocomplete tools, which suggest code as the developer types. The researchers concluded that the productivity of AI tools is weakened at later stages of software development due to “human bottlenecks.” What’s the holdup? IT Brew caught up with Greg Jennings, VP of engineering and AI at AI-native development company Anaconda, to understand what human bottlenecks stem from leveraging AI tools. While coding tools can accelerate code generation, Jennings said, they often don’t contribute to testing, validations, reviews, and other stages of the software development life cycle that still require human oversight and ultimately hold up production. “What AI coding has done is it compressed the ability to write code, so now we can write code much faster, but just because you can write code much faster doesn’t mean that you can actually do a lot of the other steps faster,” Jennings said. From cybersecurity and big data to cloud computing, IT Brew covers the latest trends shaping business tech in our 4x weekly newsletter, virtual events with industry experts, and digital guides. Sounds familiar? This isn’t the first time researchers have undermined the productivity gains of AI tools. A recent GitLab report, which surveyed 1,528 DevSecOps pros, also found that 85% believe AI has “shifted the bottleneck from writing code to reviewing and validating it.” “Compliance, security scanning, deployment, and incident response are where AI velocity stops and the rest of the life cycle waits,” the report wrote. IT Brew also previously reported on a research study from AI research nonprofit METR, which found some developers took 19% more time to complete assigned tasks when using AI coding tools. What does this all mean? Jennings said the study’s findings should be an eye-opener for tech leaders, who should readjust their expectations of how AI coding tools contribute to their bottom line moving forward. “Delivered code is not delivered value, it’s something that’s going to help us deliver more value, but now we have to pay more attention to the other steps in the process,” he said. extraction.body: One of the most senior technical leaders at a top-ten automaker said something recently that should stop anyone who thinks AI coding tools are a solved problem: "I don't know what this code does. AI wrote it for me." The context was autopilot code, with thousands of engineers to manage and resource. Dan Adler, CEO of SourceCraft, told this story on the AI Engineer podcast, and it captures the collision he sees coming for every company running large, legacy software systems. Adler's argument is counterintuitive: the AI tools that are making developers dramatically more productive are simultaneously undermining the stability of the codebases that run the world. He calls it "a tsunami of code" — code being generated faster than enterprises can review, understand, or integrate it. Adler opens with a demographic point that reframes where software actually lives. By his account, 72% of software industry workers are employed at companies with more than 500 employees — large global corporations managing thousands of repositories and decades of accumulated code. The public image of software as a startup-and-solo-founder industry, he argues, describes almost none of the real workforce. The systems these engineers maintain are unglamorous but critical: real-time transaction rejection at a bank, reimbursement-rate calculation for a dual-coverage insurance policyholder, warehouse scanning behind Amazon deliveries, Uber arrival estimates, radar-based flight-path adjustment, payroll issuance, office air conditioning running continuously. "The software that runs the world is not attractive. It is not new. It is not clean. This is how everything really works," Adler said. He frames the session explicitly as "a call to honor the people, the owners of these codebases" — the maintainers doing what he describes as "the thankless but fundamental work." The core tension Adler identifies is between generation speed and comprehension capacity. Agents are writing more code, faster, and he acknowledges their quality is improving. But the codebases receiving this output are too large to review efficiently. He rejects the obvious counterarguments — that agents can check code, that codebase-health tools exist, that model quality keeps improving — as "local maxima," dams built to contain a flow that keeps rising. The root cause is scale. Millions of lines of code across tens of thousands of repositories cannot fit in a context window or even be cloned and processed in real time. Adler calls this "simply impossible." Adler's most technically specific argument concerns how large language models actually navigate code. They "just love to search," he noted — comparing an agent to a new employee getting comfortable with a codebase — and this search behavior is how agents build their understanding. His claim is that repository architecture documented in agents.md files "changes almost nothing" in practice. The agent will search its way to understanding regardless of what documentation says. But there is a hard limit: "You can't search for something you literally can't see." Understanding requires context, and context at repository scale — 500, 5,000, 50,000, or half a million repositories — requires tooling that Adler says does not exist. He names the vendors he claims are not solving this: OpenAI, Anthropic, Cursor, and "anyone else." His concession is that their agents are "so incredibly good at solving the small tasks that most developers face every day" that demand is growing faster than ever — which is precisely why the large-scale breakdown goes unnoticed. The second unnamed quote Adler surfaces comes from a technical leader at a top-ten US bank, described as holding tens of trillions of dollars in assets in custody or under management: "Of course Claude Code can make this change, but I need to do it in 90,000 repositories." The context was a supply-chain vulnerability related to npm. The point: when agents discover and create vulnerabilities at unprecedented rates, telling a bank to use a coding agent to fix them doesn't address the problem of mapping how 90,000 repositories interact across all products. Adler's prescription is a fundamental graph of the codebase — including search and accurate compiler output — sitting in front of the agent. His formulation: "Visibility is infrastructure." The claim is that if you conduct this analysis, you empower agents to make changes effectively across the whole system rather than within a single repository. He predicts the code volume only grows: "These huge code bases are not going anywhere. In fact, there will be even more code." The question Adler does not fully answer is whether this visibility layer becomes a durable independent infrastructure business or simply a feature that frontier labs eventually fold into their own products. He acknowledges that model quality keeps improving and that major vendors will eventually add such capabilities. The tension sits unresolved. Adler announced that Sourcegraph launched its new batch-changes agent into beta on the day of the talk. The product is designed to let an owner of a massive codebase commit changes to hundreds or thousands of repositories simultaneously from a single prompt. The design principle is a split between agentic and deterministic execution: The product iteratively implements changes across the codebase, independently fixes errors, responds to CI status and pull request comments, and uses code agents where judgment is required and deterministic scripts where consistency is required. Adler emphasizes the tracking and auditing capability: confirming 100% coverage of locations needing a patch or change. The one customer proof point Adler offered comes from an early-access user at Merkari, which he describes as a global trading service from Japan with hundreds of independent microservices in production. The user was fixing a code injection issue on GitHub involving environment variables. He ran the product on two repositories where he already knew the problem existed, then let the agent explore the rest of the codebase. It found 80 more potential vulnerabilities — all in configuration files. Adler frames this as scanning and fixing in one pass via a deterministic script that guarantees consistent changes across hundreds of locations. "This is where confidence lies in the age of agent programming," he said. The unresolved question is whether this audit-and-coverage guarantee holds up at the 90,000-repository scale Adler cites as the bank's requirement. The only published proof point is a two-repository seed expanding to 80 findings. Adler's most striking framing deserves mention on its own terms: "The threat comes from within. The same tools that speed up our work and allow us to write more code faster than ever before are also creating the conditions under which these vast codebases that run our world are starting to break down." This is not an anti-AI argument. It is an argument that the adoption of AI coding tools without corresponding investment in codebase-level infrastructure is silently degrading the systems on which the global economy depends. The engineers who maintain these systems are, in Adler's words, under siege from a flood of generated code they cannot fully understand or review. Adler ends with a diagnostic for codebase owners: how many repositories do you have, how many forks, how many copies, and how many repositories have your developers brought into the company that are now used as a library or API somewhere in production without your knowledge? For the software industry, the stakes are concentrated: the same companies driving AI adoption — large enterprises with thousands of repositories — are the ones least equipped to absorb the output. Whether Sourcegraph's visibility infrastructure, or an equivalent from another vendor, becomes the standard layer for managing AI-generated code at scale will determine whether the productivity gains from AI coding tools translate into durable software quality, or into a maintenance burden that compounds with every passing day.

Adler's prescription is a fundamental graph of the codebase — including search and accurate compiler output — sitting in front of the agent. His formulation: "Visibility is infrastructure."

The claim is that if you conduct this analysis, you empower agents to make changes effectively across the whole system rather than within a single repository. He predicts the code volume only grows: "These huge code bases are not going anywhere. In fact, there will be even more code."

The question Adler does not fully answer is whether this visibility layer becomes a durable independent infrastructure business or simply a feature that frontier labs eventually fold into their own products. He acknowledges that model quality keeps improving and that major vendors will eventually add such capabilities. The tension sits unresolved.

Adler announced that Sourcegraph launched its new batch-changes agent into beta on the day of the talk. The product is designed to let an owner of a massive codebase commit changes to hundreds or thousands of repositories simultaneously from a single prompt.
The design principle is a split between agentic and deterministic execution:

The product iteratively implements changes across the codebase, independently fixes errors, responds to CI status and pull request comments, and uses code agents where judgment is required and deterministic scripts where consistency is required. Adler emphasizes the tracking and auditing capability: confirming 100% coverage of locations needing a patch or change.

The one customer proof point Adler offered comes from an early-access user at Merkari, which he describes as a global trading service from Japan with hundreds of independent microservices in production.

The user was fixing a code injection issue on GitHub involving environment variables. He ran the product on two repositories where he already knew the problem existed, then let the agent explore the rest of the codebase. It found 80 more potential vulnerabilities — all in configuration files.

Adler frames this as scanning and fixing in one pass via a deterministic script that guarantees consistent changes across hundreds of locations. "This is where confidence lies in the age of agent programming," he said.

The unresolved question is whether this audit-and-coverage guarantee holds up at the 90,000-repository scale Adler cites as the bank's requirement. The only published proof point is a two-repository seed expanding to 80 findings.

Adler's most striking framing deserves mention on its own terms: "The threat comes from within. The same tools that speed up our work and allow us to write more code faster than ever before are also creating the conditions under which these vast codebases that run our world are starting to break down."

This is not an anti-AI argument. It is an argument that the adoption of AI coding tools without corresponding investment in codebase-level infrastructure is silently degrading the systems on which the global economy depends. The engineers who maintain these systems are, in Adler's words, under siege from a flood of generated code they cannot fully understand or review.

Adler ends with a diagnostic for codebase owners: how many repositories do you have, how many forks, how many copies, and how many repositories have your developers brought into the company that are now used as a library or API somewhere in production without your knowledge?

Whether Sourcegraph's visibility infrastructure, or an equivalent from another vendor, becomes the standard layer for managing AI-generated code at scale will determine whether the productivity gains from AI coding tools translate into durable software quality, or into a maintenance burden that compounds with every passing day.

coreStoryFacts.text: The introduction of AI coding agents at a firm leads to a 30 percent increase in total lines of code generated, a 20 percent rise in the number of total commits, and a 23 percent increase in pull requests on average, the researchers write.
But all that extra code doesn’t translate directly into improved software output on the firm level.
AI agents are still a relatively new part of the coding world, of course, and there have been significant updates and upgrades to their output even since this study’s March 2026 data cutoff.

These kinds of “coding time versus review time” trade-offs could improve as software engineering teams gain more experience with the pros and cons of siccing an AI agent on particular coding problems.
Anyone who has even tangentially associated with computer programming knows that modern AI coding assistants and agents can be incredibly efficient at generating huge amounts of functional code .
For now, though, letting AI write your code looks like a double-edged sword, with increases in coding speed counteracted by similar increases in human code review time and effort.
The first large-scale empirical study of AI coding agents at enterprise scale finds that agents boost code volume by 30%, but the gains don't translate to software output.
The bottleneck is code review: review times increase 49%, revision requests nearly double, and AI review tools haven't replaced human oversight.
Researchers Fiona Chen and James Stratton analyzed data from the Jellyfish engineering analytics platform, covering 718 firms and over 725,000 workers between 2021 and 2026.

The findings are stark: while AI agents like Claude Code, Cursor, and Devin have increased code production by 30%-adding nearly 1,500 lines per worker-month-there has been no statistically significant increase in resolved Jira issues or completed epics.
When developers use AI to generate code faster, they are essentially pushing more work into the review queue.
As one senior engineer noted in the study, “We were able to write code faster in some instances, but there is only one bottleneck at a time.
The pattern is clear: firms are rushing to adopt AI agents-with adoption rates climbing from near zero in late 2024 to over 95% by early 2026-without adjusting their internal workflows.
The study found that 14% more workers are now being pulled into the code review process, placing a heavy burden on senior engineers who must vet the influx of AI-generated updates.

After examining the data and AI usage telemetry of over 100,000 GitHub developers, researchers from MIT and UPenn’s Wharton School have determined that AI coding tools might help developers produce more lines of code, but that’s not leading to more finished software shipped.

Manav Khurana, GitLab’s chief product and marketing officer, added it’s important for organizations using AI coding tools to invest in agentic infrastructure to support other steps of the software development life cycle: “If they don’t have the right agentic infrastructure to make sure that code created can become shipped software with the right level of automation, they also risk that the new code creates reliability problems, or security problems, or cost overruns, because speed sometimes also brings with it chaos.”
IT Brew caught up with Greg Jennings, VP of engineering and AI at AI-native development company Anaconda, to understand what human bottlenecks stem from leveraging AI tools.
Brianna Monsanto is a reporter for IT Brew who covers news about cybersecurity, cloud computing, and strategic IT decisions made at different companies.
Similar disparities were observed when examining developers who relied on autocomplete tools, which suggest code as the developer types.

News and intelligence for the agentic economy The first large-scale empirical study of AI coding agents at enterprise scale finds that agents boost code volume by 30%, but the gains don't translate to software output. The bottleneck is code review: review times increase 49%, revision requests nearly double, and AI review tools haven't replaced human oversight. Enterprise technology leaders are currently caught in a measurement trap. When evaluating the impact of AI coding agents, the industry has largely focused on the volume of code produced. It is an easy metric to track, but it is increasingly clear that it is the wrong one. By prioritizing output speed, firms are ignoring the reality of how software actually moves from an idea to a finished product. A new Harvard working paper , Artificial Intelligence in the Firm: Bottlenecks in Software Production , provides the first large-scale empirical evidence that this focus on volume is masking a significant operational hurdle. Researchers Fiona Chen and James Stratton analyzed data from the Jellyfish engineering analytics platform, covering 718 firms and over 725,000 workers between 2021 and 2026. The findings are stark: while AI agents like Claude Code, Cursor, and Devin have increased code production by 30%-adding nearly 1,500 lines per worker-month-there has been no statistically significant increase in resolved Jira issues or completed epics. The data reveals a disconnect between activity and outcome. While workers are pushing 20% more commits and 23% more pull requests per month, the business value-measured by resolved issues-remains flat. As one junior engineer interviewed for the study noted, “People could make a huge number of commits quickly, but code review was still the bottleneck.” The mechanism behind this is the code review process. When developers use AI to generate code faster, they are essentially pushing more work into the review queue. The data shows that review times have jumped by 49%, increasing by an average of 3.45 days. Furthermore, the share of pull requests requiring revision has nearly doubled, and the number of comments per request has risen by 35%. As one senior engineer noted in the study, “We were able to write code faster in some instances, but there is only one bottleneck at a time. If you speed up coding, the bottleneck shifts somewhere else.” This phenomenon highlights a critical flaw in how we track engineering health. We are measuring the speed of the engine while ignoring the fact that the transmission is stuck. By focusing on the wrong metrics, companies are failing to see that their investment in AI is not necessarily creating more software, but rather creating more work for the people responsible for reviewing it. The authors of the paper put it plainly: “Both technologies increase coding productivity. However, productivity gains do not fully pass through to changes in software output or employment.” The human cost of this shift is becoming increasingly apparent. The study found that 14% more workers are now being pulled into the code review process, placing a heavy burden on senior engineers who must vet the influx of AI-generated updates. This mirrors the phenomenon previously identified in our coverage of Cognition’s Devin , where the high volume of AI-written code creates a significant “babysitting tax.” Even with advanced AI tools, human oversight remains an absolute requirement, and that oversight is now consuming more time than ever. As one senior engineer emphasized, “Even with AI tools, you absolutely still need humans involved in the review process.” The pattern is clear: firms are rushing to adopt AI agents-with adoption rates climbing from near zero in late 2024 to over 95% by early 2026-without adjusting their internal workflows. Despite 80% of firms using AI-assisted review tools, only about 23% of review comments are actually AI-generated. This suggests that the heavy lifting of quality control is still falling squarely on human shoulders, even as the volume of code to review continues to climb. For engineering leaders, the implication is that the current AI adoption narrative needs a correction. As the authors note, “Realizing the benefits of AI adoption requires complementary investments in downstream review capacity, rather than simply increasing code output.” This might mean better tooling for automated testing, more efficient review workflows, or even rethinking how teams are structured to handle the increased volume of incoming code. If you speed up one part of a complex system without addressing the constraints of the next, you are not increasing productivity; you are just moving the pile of work. passages: After examining the data and AI usage telemetry of over 100,000 GitHub developers, researchers from MIT and UPenn’s Wharton School have determined that AI coding tools might help developers produce more lines of code, but that’s not leading to more finished software shipped.

Manav Khurana, GitLab’s chief product and marketing officer, added it’s important for organizations using AI coding tools to invest in agentic infrastructure to support other steps of the software development life cycle: “If they don’t have the right agentic infrastructure to make sure that code created can become shipped software with the right level of automation, they also risk that the new code creates reliability problems, or security problems, or cost overruns, because speed sometimes also brings with it chaos.”
IT Brew caught up with Greg Jennings, VP of engineering and AI at AI-native development company Anaconda, to understand what human bottlenecks stem from leveraging AI tools.
Brianna Monsanto is a reporter for IT Brew who covers news about cybersecurity, cloud computing, and strategic IT decisions made at different companies.
Similar disparities were observed when examining developers who relied on autocomplete tools, which suggest code as the developer types.

After examining the data and AI usage telemetry of over 100,000 GitHub developers, researchers from MIT and UPenn’s Wharton School have determined that AI coding tools might help developers produce more lines of code, but that’s not leading to more finished software shipped. The researchers found that synchronous agents (agents that write and edit code with the developer in real time) produced a 741% increase in lines of code and led to a 65% increase in pull requests. However, software releases only rose 20%. Similar disparities were observed when examining developers who relied on autocomplete tools, which suggest code as the developer types. The researchers concluded that the productivity of AI tools is weakened at later stages of software development due to “human bottlenecks.” What’s the holdup? IT Brew caught up with Greg Jennings, VP of engineering and AI at AI-native development company Anaconda, to understand what human bottlenecks stem from leveraging AI tools. While coding tools can accelerate code generation, Jennings said, they often don’t contribute to testing, validations, reviews, and other stages of the software development life cycle that still require human oversight and ultimately hold up production. “What AI coding has done is it compressed the ability to write code, so now we can write code much faster, but just because you can write code much faster doesn’t mean that you can actually do a lot of the other steps faster,” Jennings said. sources.title: Dan Adler Warns AI Coding Agents Are Flooding Legacy Codebases With Code No One Understands - BigGo Finance
passages: It is an argument that the adoption of AI coding tools without corresponding investment in codebase-level infrastructure is silently degrading the systems on which the global economy depends.
The engineers who maintain these systems are, in Adler's words, under siege from a flood of generated code they cannot fully understand or review.
Dan Adler, CEO of SourceCraft, told this story on the AI Engineer podcast, and it captures the collision he sees coming for every company running large, legacy software systems.
Adler's most technically specific argument concerns how large language models actually navigate code.
They "just love to search," he noted — comparing an agent to a new employee getting comfortable with a codebase — and this search behavior is how agents build their understanding.
Understanding requires context, and context at repository scale — 500, 5,000, 50,000, or half a million repositories — requires tooling that Adler says does not exist.
Agents are writing more code, faster, and he acknowledges their quality is improving.

"The software that runs the world is not attractive. It is not new. It is not clean. This is how everything really works," Adler said. He frames the session explicitly as "a call to honor the people, the owners of these codebases" — the maintainers doing what he describes as "the thankless but fundamental work." He predicts the code volume only grows: "These huge code bases are not going anywhere. In fact, there will be even more code." Adler frames this as scanning and fixing in one pass via a deterministic script that guarantees consistent changes across hundreds of locations. "This is where confidence lies in the age of agent programming," he said. The only published proof point is a two-repository seed expanding to 80 findings. Adler's most striking framing deserves mention on its own terms: "The threat comes from within. The engineers who maintain these systems are, in Adler's words, under siege from a flood of generated code they cannot fully understand or review. Whether Sourcegraph's visibility infrastructure, or an equivalent from another vendor, becomes the standard layer for managing AI-generated code at scale will determine whether the productivity gains from AI coding tools translate into durable software quality, or into a maintenance burden that compounds with every passing day.

extraction.body: Apple will announce a new smart home hub on Tuesday called the HomeView, according to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman . Over the past couple of years, we’ve seen multiple reports that Apple was working on a new smart home product , but now it seems the product has a name and a launch date. Gurman described the HomeView as a Siri-powered device with a display and an A18 chip, allowing customers to control their other smart home devices. The HomeView will reportedly be available in two models — one designed for countertops and the other to be mounted on walls. This would be Apple’s most serious bet on the smart home to date, after it failed to get much traction for its HomeKit software framework or its HomePod smart speaker. Gurman reports that on Tuesday, Apple will also be unveiling updated versions of two other home devices, namely the Apple TV set-top box and the HomePod mini. Earlier this week, he said that Apple plans to announce a partnership with LG to create a smart lock, a thermostat, and a doorbell.

sources.title: Apple's HomeView Smart Hub Launches Tuesday - First Real Challenge to Amazon Echo
passages: The company will announce its new HomeView smart home hub on Tuesday, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, marking what could be Apple's first genuine challenge to Amazon's Echo ecosystem dominance.
Unlike Amazon's retail-focused strategy or Google's advertising-driven model, Apple can position HomeView as the premium, privacy-first option that seamlessly connects with iPhones, iPads, and Macs.
Tuesday's announcement will reveal whether Apple has finally cracked the smart home code.
Apple's betting that HomeView can be that unifying force.

Success here could establish Apple as a major player in the connected home market, while failure might signal that even Apple's integration advantages can't overcome entrenched competition from Amazon and Google.
The HomeView announcement comes as Apple has been tightening security controls across its ecosystem, particularly around AI agent access.
This suggests the new hub will likely emphasize privacy and security - traditional Apple differentiators that could resonate with consumers increasingly worried about smart home data collection.
What makes this launch particularly intriguing is Apple's recent moves in AI and automation.
Apple's advantage lies in its integrated approach.
The real question is whether Apple learned from HomePod's mistakes and built something that average consumers actually want to buy.
After years of lukewarm reception for HomePod, Apple appears ready to bet big on connected home control.
For Apple, HomeView represents more than just another product launch.
Smart home adoption hit 69% of U.S. households in 2024, but the market remains frustratingly fragmented.
HomeView could be the physical manifestation of these digital capabilities, offering more sophisticated voice interactions than current smart speakers provide.

extraction.body: Apple is finally making its serious play for the smart home. The company will announce its new HomeView smart home hub on Tuesday, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, marking what could be Apple's first genuine challenge to Amazon's Echo ecosystem dominance. After years of lukewarm reception for HomePod, Apple appears ready to bet big on connected home control. Apple just dropped the news that could reshape the smart home landscape. The company's HomeView smart hub, set for Tuesday's announcement according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, represents Apple's most ambitious attempt yet to crack the connected home market that Amazon has dominated for nearly a decade. Smart home adoption hit 69% of U.S. households in 2024, but the market remains frustratingly fragmented. While Amazon's Echo devices control roughly 28% of the smart speaker market, no single platform has achieved the seamless integration that consumers actually want. Apple's betting that HomeView can be that unifying force. This marks a significant departure from Apple's previous smart home strategy. The HomePod, launched in 2018, never gained meaningful traction against cheaper alternatives from Amazon and Google. The HomePod mini helped somewhat, but Apple's smart home presence remained minimal compared to its dominance in phones and tablets. The HomeView announcement comes as Apple has been tightening security controls across its ecosystem, particularly around AI agent access. This suggests the new hub will likely emphasize privacy and security - traditional Apple differentiators that could resonate with consumers increasingly worried about smart home data collection. What makes this launch particularly intriguing is Apple's recent moves in AI and automation. The company's acquisition of AI podcast startup Huxe signals broader ambitions in AI-powered content and interaction. HomeView could be the physical manifestation of these digital capabilities, offering more sophisticated voice interactions than current smart speakers provide. The competitive landscape has shifted dramatically since HomePod's launch. Apple's advantage lies in its integrated approach. Unlike Amazon's retail-focused strategy or Google's advertising-driven model, Apple can position HomeView as the premium, privacy-first option that seamlessly connects with iPhones, iPads, and Macs. The company's 1.8 billion active devices worldwide provide a massive potential user base that competitors can't match. The Tuesday announcement will likely reveal pricing, availability, and key features. Industry insiders expect Apple to position HomeView somewhere between the $99 HomePod mini and $299 HomePod, targeting the sweet spot that made Amazon's Echo Show successful. The real question is whether Apple learned from HomePod's mistakes and built something that average consumers actually want to buy. For Apple, HomeView represents more than just another product launch. It's a statement about the company's vision for how technology should integrate into our daily lives. If successful, it could finally give Apple the smart home foothold it's been seeking for years. Apple's HomeView launch represents the company's most serious smart home challenge yet, leveraging lessons learned from HomePod's struggles and recent AI investments. Success here could establish Apple as a major player in the connected home market, while failure might signal that even Apple's integration advantages can't overcome entrenched competition from Amazon and Google. Tuesday's announcement will reveal whether Apple has finally cracked the smart home code.

As Apple explores new product categories, Gurman suggests that the company is taking a different approach to its smart home ambitions this time. The HomePod Mini and Apple TV are expected to arrive on stores on October 30. Apple’s new smart home strategy Until now, Apple has focused on developing the underlying software while relying on other companies to build compatible hardware. It would be complemented by an updated HomePod mini, powered by an S10 chip, with voice control, music playback and other functions extending throughout the home. Apple is also expected to introduce a new Apple TV set-top box powered by a standard A19 chip. The Home View is expected to come in two versions: a countertop model with a metal speaker base and a wall-mounted version with a flat base. The countertop model is expected to be available in Space Gray, Silver, Starlight and Pink, while the wall-mounted version could be limited to Space Gray and Silver. The new Apple TV is also expected to feature updated microphones that would allow users to issue Siri voice commands from across the room. Beyond the chip upgrade, the HomePod mini is expected to arrive in new colours, including Pink, White, Green, Blue and Midnight. Connected smart home ecosystem The Home View is expected to support a limited selection of Apple applications, without offering a dedicated App Store for downloading additional apps. It is also expected to work with smart home accessories developed through Apple’s partnership with LG, allowing users to control them through Siri, the Home app and other Apple devices. The accompanying devices could include a smart doorbell, a deadbolt lock, a thermostat, a temperature sensor, indoor and outdoor security cameras, and a floodlight camera. Together, these products would form a smart home starter kit. Apple appears to be developing an end-to-end system to avoid the shortcomings of its earlier smart home efforts, including the introduction of HomeKit in 2014 and the Home app in 2016. Apple plans to make these products an integral part of its broader lineup, encouraging users to adopt more devices within its ecosystem and making it easier for them to manage their connected homes through a single platform.

extraction.body: It's been over a decade since Apple's HomeKit smart home platform launched, and it is overdue for an update. ‌HomeKit‌ and the Home app can no longer keep up with AI-powered solutions from other companies like Google and Amazon, but that's set to change with a smart home revamp that Apple has planned for 2026. Apple is working on a home hub or "command center" that will serve as a centralized location for controlling smart home products, listening to music, making video calls, getting the weather, looking things up with Siri , displaying photos, making notes, viewing calendar events, and more. The device has an all-display design that resembles an iPad , with a 7-inch display. It's said to be similar in size and shape to two iPhones placed side-by-side, but Apple is designing two variants. The first version is designed to be mounted on a wall, while the second version has a speaker base that looks similar to a HomePod mini and can be placed on a desktop or countertop. The home hub will have its own operating system, and while there won't be an App Store , Apple apps will be available as widgets. Built-in sensors will be able to determine when someone is near the home hub, and the features displayed will change based on presence. If no one is by the hub, it might show information like the time and temperature, but if someone approaches, it could shift to an interface for adjusting the temperature. Presence detection will enable features like turning on the lights when someone enters the room, and it might also be able to tell one person from another. The home hub will play music, and it does have a camera that can be used for video calls. Touch-based interactions will be available for widgets, but the hub will be heavily reliant on ‌Siri‌ voice commands. ‌Siri‌ could have a personified look on the hub, with one design described as a version of the Mac Finder icon. While screen-based smart home devices like the Echo Show are available for under $200, Apple could price the home hub somewhere around $350. Price could vary for the version with the speaker base and the wall mounted version without it. Apple is aiming to launch the home hub sometime in the March to April 2026 timeframe. Apple has held off on launching the home hub because it is waiting to debut the smarter, more capable version of ‌Siri‌ that's been in the works since Apple Intelligence features launched in iOS 18. The original plan was for a better version of ‌Siri‌ to come out in an iOS 18 update, but Apple decided ‌Siri‌ just wasn't good enough to do what it wanted. ‌Siri‌ was delayed so Apple could overhaul the underlying architecture that powers the personal assistant. The new ‌Siri‌ will be more similar to ChatGPT or Claude than the ‌Siri‌ of today, incorporating large language models to answer complex queries and complete more complicated tasks. Here's what Apple originally promised ‌Siri‌ would be able to do with ‌Apple Intelligence‌: Onscreen awareness will let ‌Siri‌ see what's on your screen and complete actions involving whatever you're looking at. If someone texts you an address, for example, you can tell ‌Siri‌ to add it to their contact card. Or if you're looking at a photo and want to send it to someone, you can ask ‌Siri‌ to do it for you. Deeper app integration means that ‌Siri‌ will be able to do more in and across apps, performing actions and completing tasks that are just not possible with the personal assistant right now. We don't have a full picture of what ‌Siri‌ will be capable of, but Apple has provided a few examples of what to expect. This summer, Apple software engineering chief Craig Federighi said that transitioning ‌Siri‌ to new architecture was a success, and that the personal assistant is going to be an even bigger update than expected. "The work we've done on this end-to-end revamp of ‌‌Siri‌‌ has given us the results we needed," Federighi told employees. "This has put us in a position to not just deliver what we announced, but to deliver a much bigger upgrade than that we envisioned." Apple decided to use AI technology from Google, so ‌Siri‌ will in part be powered by a Google Gemini model that Google designed for Apple. ‌Siri‌ will be as capable as Gemini since it is using the same underlying technology, but Apple will run the model on its own Private Cloud Compute server with no information provided to Google. The new version of ‌Siri‌ is expected to be ready for an iOS 26.4 update planned for the same March or April timeframe rumored for the home hub. We're supposed to be getting updated versions of the ‌HomePod mini‌ and the Apple TV at some point between now and early 2026. Both devices will get chip upgrades, and in the case of the ‌Apple TV‌, it could gain support for some ‌Apple Intelligence‌ features. New Apple-designed networking chips will be included, but neither device is going to get a design update. The ‌HomePod mini‌ and the ‌Apple TV‌ are linked to Apple's smart home platform and serve as smart home hubs for Matter, the cross-platform protocol that opens up the number of smart home accessories that are compatible with ‌HomeKit‌. Rumors suggest that Apple is designing its own indoor security cameras that will connect to ‌HomeKit‌ and interface with the planned home hub. Cameras designed directly by Apple would offer unique integrations with Apple devices, and would offer greater privacy than competing devices because of Apple's dedication to privacy and security. Squarish 7-inch screen for controlling smart home products, listening to music, making video calls, and more. Apple's cheapest flagship model won't get an update until early 2027. The HomePod mini helped somewhat, but Apple's smart home presence remained minimal compared to its dominance in phones and tablets. The HomeView announcement comes as Apple has been tightening security controls across its ecosystem, particularly around AI agent access. This suggests the new hub will likely emphasize privacy and security - traditional Apple differentiators that could resonate with consumers increasingly worried about smart home data collection. The company's acquisition of AI podcast startup Huxe signals broader ambitions in AI-powered content and interaction. The Tuesday announcement will likely reveal pricing, availability, and key features. extraction.body: As Apple prepares to unveil a host of new products on October 13, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman has revealed several new details about the company’s plans, along with insights into its Mac and iPad event expected towards the end of October. As Apple explores new product categories, Gurman suggests that the company is taking a different approach to its smart home ambitions this time. The HomePod Mini and Apple TV are expected to arrive on stores on October 30. Apple’s new smart home strategy Until now, Apple has focused on developing the underlying software while relying on other companies to build compatible hardware. This time Apple is pursuing a more comprehensive strategy, with an integrated ecosystem and a full lineup of devices designed to work together. The new smart home hub, reportedly called the Home View, is central to this strategy. It would be complemented by an updated HomePod mini, powered by an S10 chip, with voice control, music playback and other functions extending throughout the home. Apple is also expected to introduce a new Apple TV set-top box powered by a standard A19 chip. The Home View is expected to come in two versions: a countertop model with a metal speaker base and a wall-mounted version with a flat base. The countertop model is expected to be available in Space Gray, Silver, Starlight and Pink, while the wall-mounted version could be limited to Space Gray and Silver. The new Apple TV is also expected to feature updated microphones that would allow users to issue Siri voice commands from across the room. Beyond the chip upgrade, the HomePod mini is expected to arrive in new colours, including Pink, White, Green, Blue and Midnight. Connected smart home ecosystem The Home View is expected to support a limited selection of Apple applications, without offering a dedicated App Store for downloading additional apps. It is also expected to work with smart home accessories developed through Apple’s partnership with LG, allowing users to control them through Siri, the Home app and other Apple devices. The accompanying devices could include a smart doorbell, a deadbolt lock, a thermostat, a temperature sensor, indoor and outdoor security cameras, and a floodlight camera. Together, these products would form a smart home starter kit. Apple appears to be developing an end-to-end system to avoid the shortcomings of its earlier smart home efforts, including the introduction of HomeKit in 2014 and the Home app in 2016. Apple plans to make these products an integral part of its broader lineup, encouraging users to adopt more devices within its ecosystem and making it easier for them to manage their connected homes through a single platform.

Apple’s new smart home strategy Until now, Apple has focused on developing the underlying software while relying on other companies to build compatible hardware.
This time Apple is pursuing a more comprehensive strategy, with an integrated ecosystem and a full lineup of devices designed to work together.
The new smart home hub, reportedly called the Home View, is central to this strategy.
It would be complemented by an updated HomePod mini, powered by an S10 chip, with voice control, music playback and other functions extending throughout the home.
Apple is also expected to introduce a new Apple TV set-top box powered by a standard A19 chip.
The Home View is expected to come in two versions: a countertop model with a metal speaker base and a wall-mounted version with a flat base.
The countertop model is expected to be available in Space Gray, Silver, Starlight and Pink, while the wall-mounted version could be limited to Space Gray and Silver.
The new Apple TV is also expected to feature updated microphones that would allow users to issue Siri voice commands from across the room.
Beyond the chip upgrade, the HomePod mini is expected to arrive in new colours, including Pink, White, Green, Blue and Midnight.

It is also expected to work with smart home accessories developed through Apple’s partnership with LG, allowing users to control them through Siri, the Home app and other Apple devices.
The accompanying devices could include a smart doorbell, a deadbolt lock, a thermostat, a temperature sensor, indoor and outdoor security cameras, and a floodlight camera.
Together, these products would form a smart home starter kit.
Apple appears to be developing an end-to-end system to avoid the shortcomings of its earlier smart home efforts, including the introduction of HomeKit in 2014 and the Home app in 2016.

Apple plans to make these products an integral part of its broader lineup, encouraging users to adopt more devices within its ecosystem and making it easier for them to manage their connected homes through a single platform.

extraction.body: It's been over a decade since Apple's HomeKit smart home platform launched, and it is overdue for an update. ‌HomeKit‌ and the Home app can no longer keep up with AI-powered solutions from other companies like Google and Amazon, but that's set to change with a smart home revamp that Apple has planned for 2026. Apple is working on a home hub or "command center" that will serve as a centralized location for controlling smart home products, listening to music, making video calls, getting the weather, looking things up with Siri , displaying photos, making notes, viewing calendar events, and more. The device has an all-display design that resembles an iPad , with a 7-inch display. It's said to be similar in size and shape to two iPhones placed side-by-side, but Apple is designing two variants. The first version is designed to be mounted on a wall, while the second version has a speaker base that looks similar to a HomePod mini and can be placed on a desktop or countertop. The home hub will have its own operating system, and while there won't be an App Store , Apple apps will be available as widgets. Built-in sensors will be able to determine when someone is near the home hub, and the features displayed will change based on presence. If no one is by the hub, it might show information like the time and temperature, but if someone approaches, it could shift to an interface for adjusting the temperature. Presence detection will enable features like turning on the lights when someone enters the room, and it might also be able to tell one person from another. The home hub will play music, and it does have a camera that can be used for video calls. Touch-based interactions will be available for widgets, but the hub will be heavily reliant on ‌Siri‌ voice commands. ‌Siri‌ could have a personified look on the hub, with one design described as a version of the Mac Finder icon. While screen-based smart home devices like the Echo Show are available for under $200, Apple could price the home hub somewhere around $350. Price could vary for the version with the speaker base and the wall mounted version without it. Apple is aiming to launch the home hub sometime in the March to April 2026 timeframe. Apple has held off on launching the home hub because it is waiting to debut the smarter, more capable version of ‌Siri‌ that's been in the works since Apple Intelligence features launched in iOS 18. The original plan was for a better version of ‌Siri‌ to come out in an iOS 18 update, but Apple decided ‌Siri‌ just wasn't good enough to do what it wanted. ‌Siri‌ was delayed so Apple could overhaul the underlying architecture that powers the personal assistant. The new ‌Siri‌ will be more similar to ChatGPT or Claude than the ‌Siri‌ of today, incorporating large language models to answer complex queries and complete more complicated tasks. Here's what Apple originally promised ‌Siri‌ would be able to do with ‌Apple Intelligence‌: Onscreen awareness will let ‌Siri‌ see what's on your screen and complete actions involving whatever you're looking at. If someone texts you an address, for example, you can tell ‌Siri‌ to add it to their contact card. Or if you're looking at a photo and want to send it to someone, you can ask ‌Siri‌ to do it for you. Deeper app integration means that ‌Siri‌ will be able to do more in and across apps, performing actions and completing tasks that are just not possible with the personal assistant right now. We don't have a full picture of what ‌Siri‌ will be capable of, but Apple has provided a few examples of what to expect. This summer, Apple software engineering chief Craig Federighi said that transitioning ‌Siri‌ to new architecture was a success, and that the personal assistant is going to be an even bigger update than expected. "The work we've done on this end-to-end revamp of ‌‌Siri‌‌ has given us the results we needed," Federighi told employees. "This has put us in a position to not just deliver what we announced, but to deliver a much bigger upgrade than that we envisioned." Apple decided to use AI technology from Google, so ‌Siri‌ will in part be powered by a Google Gemini model that Google designed for Apple. ‌Siri‌ will be as capable as Gemini since it is using the same underlying technology, but Apple will run the model on its own Private Cloud Compute server with no information provided to Google. The new version of ‌Siri‌ is expected to be ready for an iOS 26.4 update planned for the same March or April timeframe rumored for the home hub. We're supposed to be getting updated versions of the ‌HomePod mini‌ and the Apple TV at some point between now and early 2026. Both devices will get chip upgrades, and in the case of the ‌Apple TV‌, it could gain support for some ‌Apple Intelligence‌ features. New Apple-designed networking chips will be included, but neither device is going to get a design update. The ‌HomePod mini‌ and the ‌Apple TV‌ are linked to Apple's smart home platform and serve as smart home hubs for Matter, the cross-platform protocol that opens up the number of smart home accessories that are compatible with ‌HomeKit‌. Rumors suggest that Apple is designing its own indoor security cameras that will connect to ‌HomeKit‌ and interface with the planned home hub. Cameras designed directly by Apple would offer unique integrations with Apple devices, and would offer greater privacy than competing devices because of Apple's dedication to privacy and security.
